entries.title: Attorney General & 2 Others v David Ndii & 79 Others
entries.principle: A constitutional amendment process must comply with the Constitution's own architecture, including public participation and the allocation of constituent power.
entries.facts: An application by the Attorney General seeking a stay of the High Court's BBI judgment.
entries.holding: A constitutional amendment process must comply with the Constitution's own architecture, including public participation and the allocation of constituent power.
entries.judges: Mutunga CJ, Ibrahim, Ojwang, Wanjala and Ndung'u SCJJ (Supreme Court)

entries.title: Mitu-Bell Welfare Society v Kenya Airports Authority & 2 Others
entries.principle: Forced evictions must be carried out in a manner consistent with human dignity; the State must provide adequate notice, consultation and resettlement, and resource constraints cannot excuse indignity.
entries.facts: A petition by evicted residents of Mitumba village near Wilson Airport seeking redress for forced eviction.
entries.holding: Forced evictions must be carried out in a manner consistent with human dignity; the State must provide adequate notice, consultation and resettlement, and resource constraints cannot excuse indignity.
entries.judges: Mwilu DCJ, Ibrahim, Wanjala, Ndung'u and Lenaola SCJJ (Supreme Court)

entries.title: Ndii & others v Attorney General & others
entries.citation: [2021] KEHC 9746 (KLR) (13 May 2021) (Consolidated Petitions E282, 397, E400, E401, E402, E416 and E426 of 2020)
entries.court: High Court of Kenya (Constitutional and Human Rights Division)
entries.principle: A constitutional amendment process must comply with the Constitution's own architecture, including the requirement of public participation and the allocation of constituent power; a process that bypasses those requirements is invalid.
entries.facts: Consolidated petitions challenged the Building Bridges Initiative (BBI) constitutional amendment process. The petitioners alleged that the process bypassed constitutional requirements. The case raised questions of public participation, constituent power and the amendment process.
entries.holding: A constitutional amendment process must comply with the Constitution's own architecture, including public participation and the allocation of constituent power; a process that bypasses those requirements is invalid.
entries.judges: Mwita, Ong'udi and Ngaah JJ (High Court)
entries.note: Popularly known as the BBI judgment. Verify the current appellate status before relying on it.

entries.title: In the Matter of the Principle of Gender Representation in the National Assembly and the Senate
entries.principle: Article 81(b) creates a binding constitutional obligation to secure the two-thirds gender principle; its realisation is progressive and requires legislative and policy measures, not judicial legislation.
entries.facts: The Attorney General sought an advisory opinion on the principle of gender representation in the National Assembly and the Senate. The reference concerned Article 81(b) of the Constitution and the obligation to achieve the two-thirds gender principle. The Court was asked to determine whether the principle was immediately enforceable or progressively realisable.
entries.holding: Article 81(b) creates a binding constitutional obligation to secure the two-thirds gender principle; its realisation is progressive and requires legislative and policy measures, not judicial legislation.
entries.judges: Mutunga CJ, Tunoi, Ibrahim, Ojwang, Wanjala and Ndung'u SCJJ (Supreme Court)

entries.principle: Articles 27 and 81(b) permit, and in appropriate circumstances require, temporary special measures to remedy structural inequality; administrative inconvenience does not justify indefinite delay.
entries.facts: The Centre for Rights Education and Awareness petitioned for the implementation of the two-thirds gender principle in public appointments. entries.holding: Articles 27 and 81(b) permit, and in appropriate circumstances require, temporary special measures to remedy structural inequality; administrative inconvenience does not justify indefinite delay.

entries.title: Federation of Women Lawyers Kenya (FIDA-K) & 5 others v Attorney General & 3 others
entries.principle: Customary law is subordinate to the Constitution; customary practices that deny women equal protection in succession and family matters cannot survive the guarantees of equality and non-discrimination.
entries.facts: The Federation of Women Lawyers challenged customary law provisions on succession that discriminated against women. The petitioners alleged that customary practices denied women equal protection in inheritance matters. The case raised questions of the relationship between customary law and the Constitution.
entries.holding: Customary law is subordinate to the Constitution; customary practices that deny women equal protection in succession and family matters cannot survive the guarantees of equality and non-discrimination.
